# Minimum simplex containers can have unbounded convexification cost

There is no constant \(B_{1,2}\) of the proposed kind, even with
exactly three positive actual fibers and no new integer bases after
convexification. The same counterexample repeats to every \(n\ge1\)
with \(d=2\). The obstruction is the first-order support mismatch
between a minimum triangle around a small square and the three
fixed facet normals of a larger, differently shaped triangle.

All coordinates and the fiber family below are exact. The proof
uses an attained positive compact support gap, not a numerical
optimization or a conjectured description of minimum triangles.

## 1. The actual three-fiber family

Let
\[
Q=[0,1]^2,\qquad
T=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(1,0),(0,2)\},\qquad |T|=1.
\]
For \(0<\epsilon\le1\), take the full-dimensional convex body
\[
C_\epsilon=\operatorname{conv}
\bigl((\{0\}\times T)\cup(\{2\}\times\epsilon Q)\bigr)
\subset\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2.
\tag{1}
\]
Its projection is \([0,2]\), and its actual integer fibers are
\[
K_0=T,\qquad K_1=(T+\epsilon Q)/2,\qquad K_2=\epsilon Q.
\tag{2}
\]
All three are full dimensional. Formula (2) follows directly
from grouping any convex combination according to its endpoint
base. Thus the source is compatible and lattice-complete.

Write \(\Gamma=4/9\), and use the actual ordinary deficits
\[
\delta_j=|K_j|\,[D(K_j)-\Gamma].
\tag{3}
\]
They are nonnegative by ordinary Grünbaum. We will show
\[
0<\sum_{j=0}^2\delta_j\le\frac7{36}\epsilon^2,
\tag{4}
\]
whereas convexifying ANY choices of minimum enclosing triangles
adds at least \(c\epsilon\) mixed area, with \(c>0\) fixed.

## 2. Every ordinary deficit is accounted for

The triangle \(T\) has \(D(T)=\Gamma\), so \(\delta_0=0\).
The square is centrally symmetric, and its centroid has depth
\(1/2\); complementary caps bound every candidate's depth by
\(1/2\). Therefore
\[
\delta_2=\epsilon^2(1/2-4/9)=\epsilon^2/18.
\tag{5}
\]

The Minkowski sum \(M_\epsilon=T+\epsilon Q\) is the pentagon
with vertices
\[
(0,0),\ (1+\epsilon,0),\ (1+\epsilon,\epsilon),\
(\epsilon,2+\epsilon),\ (0,2+\epsilon).
\]
Its area and a convenient enclosing triangle are
\[
|M_\epsilon|=1+3\epsilon+\epsilon^2,\qquad
U_\epsilon=\{x,y\ge0:\ 2x+y\le2+3\epsilon\},
\]
\[
|U_\epsilon|=1+3\epsilon+\frac94\epsilon^2,\qquad
|U_\epsilon|-|M_\epsilon|=\frac54\epsilon^2.
\tag{6}
\]

For every point in \(M_\epsilon\subset U_\epsilon\), one
canonical through-point triangle cap has \(U_\epsilon\)-area
at most \(\Gamma|U_\epsilon|\): some barycentric coordinate
of the point is at least \(1/3\). Its \(M_\epsilon\)-area is
no greater. Taking the maximum over all actual candidates gives
an absolute depth bound, and scaling by \(1/2\) gives
\[
\delta_1
\le\frac{\Gamma}{4}\bigl(|U_\epsilon|-|M_\epsilon|\bigr)
=\frac5{36}\epsilon^2.
\tag{7}
\]
Together (5) and (7) prove (4). This upper bound includes all
oblique caps through every middle candidate; it uses an actual
upper cover, not an assumed formula for the middle maximum.
An exact value of \(D(K_1)\) is unnecessary.

## 3. A strict support gap for every minimum square container

For a compact convex set \(S\), define
\[
p_T(S)=2h_S(-e_1)+h_S(-e_2)+h_S(2e_1+e_2).
\tag{8}
\]
These are the three edge-length-weighted support values of \(T\).
For \(Q\) one has \(p_T(Q)=3\).

Consider the family \(\mathcal A\) of all full-dimensional
triangles \(S\) with \(Q\subseteq S\) and \(|S|\le2\).
It is nonempty: \(\operatorname{conv}(0,2e_1,2e_2)\) is one
member. It contains EVERY minimum-area enclosing triangle of
\(Q\), since this displayed competitor has area two.

The family is compact in the Hausdorff topology, including its
triangle vertex parameters. Indeed \(Q\) contains the radius
\(1/2\) disk about \(c_Q=(1/2,1/2)\). For any vertex \(v\)
of \(S\), the cone from the disk's diameter perpendicular to
\(v-c_Q\) has area \(|v-c_Q|/2\) and is contained in \(S\).
Consequently \(|v-c_Q|\le4\). A limiting vertex triple still
contains \(Q\), hence remains full dimensional, and preserves
the area upper bound.

For \(S\in\mathcal A\), each support term in
\[
p_T(S)-3
=2h_S(-e_1)+h_S(-e_2)+[h_S(2e_1+e_2)-3]
\tag{9}
\]
is nonnegative, because \(S\) contains \(Q\).
Equality would force
\[
Q\subseteq S\subseteq
R=\{x,y\ge0:\ 2x+y\le3\}.
\tag{10}
\]
The square's positive-length segments on \(x=0\) and \(y=0\)
then force these lines to be two facets of the triangle \(S\).
Their common vertex is the origin, so
\[
S=\operatorname{conv}(0,(a,0),(0,b))
\]
for some \(a,b>0\). Inclusion in \(R\) gives
\(a\le3/2,\ b\le3\), while \((1,1)\in S\) gives
\(1/a+1/b\le1\). The reverse inequality
\(1/a+1/b\ge2/3+1/3=1\) forces \(a=3/2,b=3\).
Thus \(S=R\) and \(|S|=9/4>2\), a contradiction.

Continuity of (8) on the compact nonempty family therefore gives
the exact, attained dimension-specific constant
\[
\alpha=\min_{S\in\mathcal A}[p_T(S)-3]>0.
\tag{11}
\]
No classification or uniqueness of minimum square containers
has been assumed. The compact-gap proof is uniform over all
their possible choices.

## 4. Exact convexification growth

For any triangle \(S\), the planar Minkowski area identity gives
\[
|T+\epsilon S|
=|T|+\epsilon p_T(S)+\epsilon^2|S|.
\tag{12}
\]
For clarity, this identity is elementary for polygons. Merge
their cyclic lists of edge directions to describe \(T+\epsilon S\).
Each resulting vertex is affine in \(\epsilon\), so the shoelace
area is a quadratic polynomial for \(\epsilon>0\). Its constant
coefficient is \(|T|\), its leading coefficient is \(|S|\),
and its linear coefficient is the sum over edges of \(T\) of
edge length times \(h_S\) at the outward unit normal. The latter
coefficient follows by the first-order parallel edge strips;
all corner corrections are quadratic. For this \(T\), those
three terms are exactly (8). Parallel coincident edge directions
can be merged; they cause no change to the identity.

Now choose arbitrary minimum enclosing triangles \(S_j\) for
the three actual fibers in (2), and let
\[
L_\epsilon=\operatorname{conv}
\bigcup_{j=0}^2(\{j\}\times S_j).
\]
The exact triangle \(K_0=T\) has the unique minimum container
\(S_0=T\). Scaling shows \(S_2=\epsilon S\), where \(S\)
is some minimum container of \(Q\), hence belongs to
\(\mathcal A\). The middle actual fiber of \(L_\epsilon\)
contains \((T+\epsilon S)/2\), irrespective of the choice of
the middle minimum container \(S_1\).

Using (6), (11), and (12), and \(|S|\ge|Q|=1\), gives
\[
|(L_\epsilon)_1|-|K_1|
\ge\frac14\bigl[|T+\epsilon S|-|T+\epsilon Q|\bigr]
\]
\[
=\frac14\left[\epsilon(p_T(S)-3)
+\epsilon^2(|S|-1)\right]
\ge\frac{\alpha}{4}\epsilon.
\tag{13}
\]
Every other fiber excess is nonnegative. The projection of
\(L_\epsilon\) is still \([0,2]\), so there are no additional
integer bases to omit. All comparisons concern its ACTUAL
fibers after taking the hull.

Combining (4) and (13) proves, for EVERY choice of minimum
containers and hence after optimizing those choices,
\[
\frac{\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z}
(|(L_\epsilon)_z|-|K_z|)}
{\sum_{j=0}^2|K_j|\,[D(K_j)-\Gamma]}
\ge\frac{9\alpha}{7\epsilon}
\longrightarrow\infty.
\tag{14}
\]
The denominator is positive by (5). This refutes any finite
\(B_{1,2}\).

## 5. Scope and additional integer coordinates

For \(n>1\), take the product of the actual body (1) with
\([0,1]^{n-1}\) in the additional INTEGER base coordinates.
Every resulting binary layer has the same three fibers.
At a fixed binary vertex, any convex combination contributing
to that layer must use only vertices with the same binary
coordinates. Therefore every layer retains the lower bound
(13), even if different minimum containers are chosen in
different layers. Both the summed deficits and the lower
bound on added mass are multiplied by \(2^{n-1}\). Formula
(14) consequently also refutes every finite \(B_{n,2}\),
for each \(n\ge1\).

For \(d=1\), in contrast, each positive compact convex fiber
is already an interval, its unique minimum simplex container
is itself, and the proposed convexification adds nothing.
No higher-dimensional extension is needed for the obstruction
proved here.

The example is not an OC counterexample. It disproves the
specific quantitative bridge from small total own-fiber depth
deficits to the cost of convexifying minimum simplex containers.
The original source is a fully compatible family throughout.
